cards.name: Abandoned cart / browse abandonment email
cards.summary: A triggered email (usually a 2-3 email flow) that brings a shopper back to the exact product they left. Good ones read like a helpful shop assistant: they show the item, remove the one doubt that stopped checkout, and give one button back to the cart.
use_for: cart abandonment flow (2-3 emails) for a Shopify/WooCommerce D2C store
browse abandonment (viewed a product, never added to cart)
checkout abandonment where payment failed or COD was not offered
the email leg of an email + WhatsApp + SMS recovery sequence
avoid: Leading with a discount in email 1: it trains repeat visitors to abandon on purpose. Lead with the product and the doubt it removes; hold any incentive for the last email and only if margins allow.

Fake scarcity ('Only 2 left!', '30 people are viewing this') that is not wired to live stock data: it is a false-urgency dark pattern under India's CCPA 2023 guidelines. Show stock or deadlines only when the data is real.
Guilt or nagging copy ('You forgot something, again?'). Use a neutral reminder and a reason to come back.
Promotional newsletters disguised as recovery: if the cart item is not visible above the fold, write a promotional email instead (genre:promotional_email).

cards.goal: Click back to the saved cart and complete checkout.

structure.does: Names the product or the cart and pairs with a preheader that adds a reason (delivery date, COD, easy returns). No 'Hey!' or 'Oops'.
Plain reminder in the brand's voice that the item is saved; one sentence, no guilt.
Dynamic product image, name, variant (size/colour), price and quantity from the ESP's cart tokens; the visual carries the sell.

Answers the one objection most likely to stop checkout for this category: size fit, delivery date to the shopper's pin code, COD or UPI, returns window, authenticity. Email 2 can use a short review instead.
One button whose label says the action ('Return to my cart', 'Complete my order'), repeated once at most.
A human route for stuck buyers (WhatsApp number, reply-to, support hours), useful when payment failed.
Brand address, unsubscribe and preference links as the ESP requires.

length.note: Per email body, excluding the cart block. Browse abandonment sits at the short end; high-ticket or considered purchases (furniture, electronics) earn the long end with one proof element. Flow = 2-3 emails; set timing in the ESP and test it.

checklist: Does the subject line name the product, the cart or the brand (not just 'Hey!' or 'Oops')?
Does the preheader add new information instead of repeating the subject?
Is the product (name, variant, price) shown via cart tokens near the top?
Is there exactly one primary CTA, labelled with the action (not 'Click here')?
Does the email answer at least one specific purchase doubt (delivery, COD/UPI, returns, size, authenticity)?
Is email 1 free of discounts?
Is every deadline or stock statement true and data-driven?
Is a human help route given (WhatsApp, reply-to or support line)?
Is the tone free of guilt or shaming?
Are the unsubscribe link and sender details present?
pitfalls: Hard-coding product names: the flow sends the wrong item. Use the ESP's cart/line-item tokens and preview with a real abandoned cart.
Three emails that all say 'still thinking?': give each email a different job (reminder, doubt remover, last nudge or incentive).
Ignoring the Indian payment reality: many checkouts die at payment. Mention COD/UPI or 'payment failed? reply and we'll help' when the store supports it.
WhatsApp and email firing the same message minutes apart: stagger channels and suppress the email once the order is placed.

ban.label: spam-trigger or pushy phrasing

cards.exemplar_brief: Email 1 of a 3-email abandoned-cart flow for a Pune D2C cotton kurta brand (orders Rs 1,200-2,500, COD and UPI available, 7-day exchange, ships in 2-4 days); audience: first-time visitors who left one kurta in the cart; English with one light Hinglish line; subject + preheader + 70-120 word body using cart tokens; no discount; goal: return to cart and complete checkout.

'Payment atak gaya tha?' is natural Hinglish. Only nit: subject is the stock pattern and can run long with real kurta names; keep item.name short or truncate.

cards.name: About page / company bio
cards.summary: The page a prospect opens to decide whether to trust you. A good About page leads with who you help and why you exist, proves it with specifics (years, clients, names, faces), tells one real origin moment, and ends with a single next step.
use_for: About us page for an SME, clinic, CA or law firm, agency or D2C brand
'Our story' page for a founder-led brand
company bio for proposals, tender documents and LinkedIn company pages (cut down)
rewriting a generic About page that does not convert
avoid: Opening with 'Founded in 2009, XYZ is a leading...': the reader wants to know what's in it for them. Open with who you serve and the problem you fix, then the history.
Value lists ('Integrity. Innovation. Excellence.') with no example: show each value in one concrete act or cut it.
Unprovable superlatives ('India's best', 'No. 1 firm'): ASCI and the Consumer Protection Act require claims to be substantiated. Replace with a checkable fact.
A personal founder essay when the buyer is choosing a firm: keep the founder story to one paragraph and link to a separate founder bio (genre:professional_bio).

cards.goal: Trust the business enough to take the next step (call, book, enquire or buy).

structure.does: Says who you help and the result, in the customer's words; 'About us' can be the nav label, not the headline.
The customer's problem and why this business exists to solve it; the reader should recognise themselves.
One specific moment that started the business (place, year, the trigger), told in 3-5 sentences, ending in what it made you decide.
2-4 concrete differences in method, each with proof: a number with its time window, a named client type, a certification, a process step.
Founder and key team with names, roles, photos and one human detail each; for larger firms, leaders only plus a team photo.
Client logos, 1-2 short testimonials with name and role, press mentions, years and numbers served.
One next step that matches buying stage ('Book a 20-minute call', 'See our work', 'WhatsApp us').

length.note: Professional firms with team bios and a long track record run long; one-person brands and D2C stores run short. Every paragraph must survive the question 'would a buyer miss this?'.

checklist: Does the first screen say who the business helps and what they get?
Is there at least one specific origin detail (place, year, a real moment)?
Does every experience claim carry a number, name or time window?
Are real people named with roles (or is there a stated reason not to)?
If values are listed, does each have a concrete example?
Is the page free of unprovable superlatives ('best', 'No. 1', 'leading') or are they sourced?
Does the opening use more 'you' than 'we'?
Is there exactly one primary next step?
pitfalls: Writing it from the founder's diary: the timeline of every office move bores buyers. Keep only events that explain why a client should trust you today.
Stock-photo team: faces sell trust. If the client will not supply photos, write fewer people with more detail rather than a faceless list.
Copying the homepage: the About page is where the evidence lives; the homepage is where the offer lives. Cross-link instead of repeating.
Year-stamped numbers that rot ('500+ clients'): write '500+ clients since 2009' and note in the hand-off which numbers need yearly updating.
cards.exemplar_brief: About page for 'Bhandari & Mehra Associates' (demo name), a 12-person chartered accountancy firm in Jaipur, founded 2009 by partners Ritu Bhandari (ICAI-qualified CA, runs GST and export refunds) and Sandeep Mehra (CA, runs income-tax notices and audit); handles GST, income-tax notices and export compliance for D2C and export SMEs; 300+ active clients. Founding moment (use as the origin story): in March 2009 a Jaipur gem exporter got an income-tax notice with a 7-day reply window; his old firm answered on day six with a wrong figure. Ritu and Sandeep, then colleagues at a mid-size Jaipur audit firm, rebuilt his workings over one weekend, replied on time, and decided to start a practice where a partner reads every notice within one working day. Proof: partner reads every notice within one working day; one team handles GST, ITR and refunds so the figures agree; 40+ exporters on LUT/IGST refund files. Human details: Ritu coaches a Saturday-morning girls' cricket group; Sandeep still hand-writes his client call list. One testimonial: 'They found the mismatch in our GSTR-1 in an afternoon' - Pooja Agarwal, finance head, a Jaipur home-textile exporter (demo). Audience: founders of Rs 5-50 crore businesses comparing 2-3 firms; English; 400-550 words; goal: book a 20-minute consultation.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Headline plus subhead say who and what; opening is 'you'-led and recognisable (unopened GST notice, stuck refund, CA who answers on day four); three differences with real mechanics (one team so GSTR-1/ITR/refund figures agree, written first read of a notice, marketplace TCS and LUT/IGST refund detail); one CTA. Origin moment, partner names and testimonial are placeholders (not supplied). Writer fault: 'FCA' for both partners was invented. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply the two partners' names and the founding moment (one line: the client or notice that made them start, 2009), since the structure's Origin story part cannot be written without it. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now supplies partner names/roles, the 2009 founding moment, proof points, human details and a testimonial; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Advertorial / sponsored article
cards.summary: A paid article that reads like the host publication's own journalism and still moves the reader to the brand. It works when most of it is genuinely useful (a news peg, an explainer, real data) and the brand arrives as one credible part of the answer, with the paid label in plain sight.
use_for: sponsored article on a news, finance, lifestyle or trade site ('Partner content', 'Brand Desk')
print advertorial pages in newspapers and magazines
long-form native piece for a brand's paid media plan
sponsored feature in a trade newsletter
avoid: Hiding the paid nature: unlabelled paid content misleads readers and breaks ad self-regulation. Put the label above the headline.

Writing a press release with a news headline: if the brand is in the headline and every paragraph, readers bounce. Lead with the reader's problem or the news; bring the brand in after the reader cares.
Sensational 'doctors hate this' headlines: they belong to low-quality native ad networks and damage the host's trust. Use the publication's real headline style.
Followed paid links: Google treats paid articles with links that pass ranking credit as link spam unless the links carry rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow".

cards.goal: Read to the end, believe the brand is a credible answer, and act on the soft CTA (visit, calculate, sign up).

structure.does: Publication's own label ('Partner content', 'Brand Desk', 'Advt.', 'Sponsored') above or beside the headline.
Written in the host's headline style around the reader's question or a news peg, not the brand name.
A scene, a person or a striking fact that makes the problem real.
Why this matters now, to this reader; sets up the article's promise.
Explainer, tips, data or expert view that helps even a reader who never buys; subheads every 150-250 words.
Introduce the brand as one answer: what it does, how it works, price or plan, with a named customer, expert quote or sourced number.
A next step in the publication's voice (calculator, free guide, store locator), with a sponsored-tagged link.

length.note: Print length is fixed by page size and images; online native pieces run longer. The publication's own average feature length is the best guide.

checklist: Is a paid label visible at or above the headline?
Would the headline sit naturally on the host's editorial page?
Is the brand absent from the headline and the first paragraph?
Would a reader who never buys still learn something specific?
Is every number and claim sourced or attributable to a named person?
Is the brand section concrete (what, how, price or plan, proof)?
Is there one soft CTA, and are paid links marked sponsored or nofollow?
Is it free of miracle, guarantee and 'secret' language?
pitfalls: Client rewrites that add the brand name to every paragraph: agree the 60/30/10 split (useful/brand/CTA) in the brief before drafting.
Unverifiable health or returns claims ('guaranteed 12% returns', 'cures diabetes') turn an advertorial into a misleading ad. Use the regulator-approved wording or cut the claim.
Ignoring the host's style sheet: match its spelling, number style and headline case so the piece reads native.
Fake bylines or 'staff reporter' credits: credit 'Brand Desk' or the brand's expert, never a fictional journalist.
cards.exemplar_brief: Online advertorial ('Partner content') for BimaBridge (demo name), a Bengaluru health-insurance comparison platform (IRDAI-licensed web aggregator; licence line to print: 'BimaBridge Insurance Web Aggregator Pvt Ltd, IRDAI licence no. WA-0000 (demo), valid till 31 March 2028; insurance is the subject matter of solicitation'), on a personal-finance news site. Topic: what a super top-up policy is and when salaried 30-45-year-olds supporting retired parents need one. English; 700-900 words; soft CTA to the platform's free premium calculator (compares 14 insurers; free to the user; BimaBridge is paid by insurers). Advisor quote supplied by the client, to use verbatim: 'Most families I meet hold a Rs 5 lakh cover from the employer and think they are done. One hip surgery for a parent can cross that in a week. A super top-up only starts paying after the first Rs 5 lakh is used, so it costs far less than raising the base cover.' - Kavita Narang, independent insurance advisor, 12 years in practice, IRDAI-licensed individual agent (demo). One illustrative number, from the calculator, checked 5 Oct 2026: Rs 50 lakh super top-up with a Rs 5 lakh deductible, 38-year-old non-smoker, about Rs 6,500 a year. Facts the writer may use: IRDAI's 2024 cap of three years on pre-existing-disease waiting periods; Section 80D deduction (old tax regime only). Goal: reader understands super top-ups and uses the calculator.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Reads like the host's own explainer: paid label, reader-question headline (17 words, over the 8-14 band), composite Bengaluru scene lede, nut graf, subheaded body (top-up vs super top-up worked example, when it fits, 5 checks), brand only after ~80% as one answer, sponsored-tagged calculator CTA, solicitation disclaimer. Facts check out (IRDAI 2024 three-year PED cap, 80D old regime). 'Insurance advisors point to' is a soft attribution. Brand section ~17% and placeholder-heavy. cards.name: Affiliate review / affiliate article
cards.summary: A single-product review (or 'is it worth it') article whose links earn a commission. It succeeds when it reads like advice from someone who actually used the product: test conditions, measurements, honest cons, who should skip it, and a clear verdict, with the affiliate disclosure up front.
use_for: single-product review ('X review after 30 days')
'Is X worth it?' and 'X vs Y' money pages
review section of a commerce or affiliate blog
Amazon/Flipkart affiliate content for a niche site
avoid: Rewriting the manufacturer's spec sheet: Google's review guidance asks for first-hand evidence and quantitative measurements, and thin rewrites get demoted. If you have not used it, write a comparison of published specs and say so.
Only pros: a review with no real cons reads as an ad and loses trust. Name at least one real drawback and who it matters to.
Disclosure hidden in the footer: put it before the first affiliate link in plain words ('We earn a commission if you buy through these links').
Ranking many products in one piece: that is a best-of roundup (genre:best_of_roundup).

cards.goal: Decide whether the product fits their need and click through to buy it, or to the better-fitting alternative.

structure.does: Plain-language affiliate disclosure before the first link.
Who it's for, who should skip it, score or one-line verdict, price with the date checked, primary link.
Duration, setting, conditions and what was measured, with original photos referenced.
Each strength backed by an observation or measurement from the test, in the buyer's use case.
Real cons, how much they matter and to whom.
1-3 rivals: when to pick each instead, with links.
Which variant, what to check (warranty, service network, filters/consumables cost), 3-5 real questions buyers ask.
Restates who should buy and links to the product (and the alternative).

length.note: Driven by product complexity and the number of buyer questions; a Rs 500 gadget does not need 2,500 words, a laptop or air purifier might.

checklist: Does an affiliate disclosure appear before the first affiliate link?
Does the piece state how long and in what conditions the product was used?
Are there at least two measured or observed facts from the test (not from the spec sheet)?
Is at least one real con named, with who it matters to?
Is at least one alternative compared, with when to choose it?
Does it say who should not buy?
Is the price given with the date it was checked?
Is the verdict stated both near the top and at the end?
pitfalls: Inventing test results: if the client supplies no test data, ask for it or reframe the piece as a spec comparison; never fabricate measurements.
Stale prices and 'deal' language: prices on Indian marketplaces change daily. Write 'Rs 12,999 on Amazon.in when checked on 3 Oct 2026' and avoid 'lowest price ever'.
Ignoring after-sales: Indian buyers weigh service network, warranty claims and consumable costs (filters, refills). Cover them.
Affiliate link on every mention: link the first mention, the verdict box and the final CTA; more looks spammy.
cards.exemplar_brief: Affiliate review of the 'PureBreeze 400' (demo name), a Rs 13,000 HEPA air purifier (price checked on Amazon.in 5 Oct 2026: Rs 12,999), for a Delhi-NCR home-appliance blog; audience: parents in Delhi flats buying before winter smog. Tester notes supplied: 21 days in a 160 sq ft bedroom, windows and door shut, incense burnt to push PM2.5 up, readings from a separate Rs 3,500 handheld PM2.5 meter 2 m away; PM2.5 fell from about 180 to 35 in 40 minutes on high; 52 dB on high and 33 dB on low (sleep mode); replacement filter Rs 2,800 every 6-8 months; app needs 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (failed on a 5 GHz-only router), shows live PM2.5, scheduling works, logged out twice in 21 days. Cheaper alternative to name in the comparison: 'AirNest 300' (demo), Rs 9,500 (checked 5 Oct 2026), rated for 130 sq ft, CADR 280 m3/h vs 400 for the PureBreeze, 58 dB on high, no app, filter Rs 1,900 every 6 months; fits a small room or a tighter budget. English with Indian context; 1,300-1,700 words; Amazon.in affiliate links; goal: click through to this model or the cheaper alternative. The editorial score out of 10 is the writer's call.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1.Structure complete (disclosure before first link, verdict box, method, strengths from the supplied notes, honest cons, alternative, buying advice, parent FAQ, verdict top and bottom); filter running-cost maths and the 2.4 GHz fix are exactly what a Delhi parent needs; NAAQS 60 ug/m3 context is correct. Writer faults: invented test conditions not in the notes (windows shut, door closed, 'did not light anything', run schedule, 'as long as the door stayed shut'), which the card's pitfall forbids; 'Rs 12,600-16,800 over three years: more than the purifier itself' is false at the low end (12,600 < 13,000); '[X/10]' score left as a placeholder though the score is an editorial call. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> name the cheaper alternative with price, date checked and 2-3 specs (the goal sends readers to it but the brief never names it), and add the low-setting dB and app notes. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now names the cheaper alternative (price, date, specs), adds low-setting dB, app notes and the test conditions; re-judge pending.

cards.name: AI video / film prompt-script (shot-by-shot)
cards.summary: A shot list written as prompts an AI video model can execute: per shot, a fixed character and location description, one action, camera, lens, light, audio and duration. A good one produces usable, consistent shots in one or two generations because nothing is left for the model to guess and nothing changes between shots by accident.
use_for: AI-generated ads and brand films (9:16 reels, 16:9 films)
music videos and AI short films
storyboard-to-video handoff for an AI production team
explainer B-roll generated shot by shot
avoid: Mood words instead of instructions ('epic, stunning, cinematic, 8K'): the model cannot film adjectives. Name the shot size, camera move, lens and light source.
Re-describing the character differently in each shot: drift follows. Write one descriptor string per character and paste it verbatim into every shot.
Several actions in one shot ('she enters, sits, opens the letter and cries'): models blend or drop actions. One main action per shot; split the rest.
Real people, celebrities or brand logos without rights: use original characters and the client's own assets, and plan the AI-content label.

cards.goal: Generate each shot as intended in one or two attempts, with characters and look consistent across the whole film.

structure.does: Project, target model/tool, aspect ratio, resolution, total runtime, shot count, style reference (film look, grade), language of any dialogue.
One fixed descriptor per character (age, build, face, hair, wardrobe with colours) and per location (place, time of day, light), each with an ID to paste into shots.
Shot number, duration, shot size and angle, camera movement in film terms (static, slow push-in, tracking left, handheld).
Pasted character descriptor and ONE main action with timing ('over 4 seconds she turns toward the door').
Lens/focal length and depth of field, light source and direction, colour palette, texture (film grain, haze).
Dialogue in quotes with speaker and language, SFX, ambience, music cue; or 'no dialogue'.
What must not appear (on-screen text, extra people, logos), and which reference image or previous frame anchors continuity.
Transitions, VO/subtitle lines, end card and the AI-content label plan for publishing.

length.note: Per shot prompt 40-130 words excluding the pasted character and location descriptors (each 30-60 words, pasted into every shot they appear in). Shot count = runtime divided by the model's clip length (check the tool's current maximum clip duration and prompt limits before writing). Longer prompts are not better; every word should be an instruction.

checklist: Does the header state model, aspect ratio, runtime and shot count?
Is each character's descriptor identical (copy-pasted) in every shot they appear in?
Does every shot state its duration?
Does every shot have exactly one main action?
Is the camera described in film terms (shot size + movement)?
Is a light source and direction named in every shot?
Are dialogue lines in quotes with speaker and language?
Are shots 2+ anchored to a reference image or previous frame?
Is the script free of real people's likenesses and third-party logos unless rights are confirmed?
Is an AI-content disclosure planned for publishing?
pitfalls: Asking the model to render on-screen text or brand names: most video models garble text. Add titles in the edit and write 'no on-screen text' in the constraints.
Continuity by memory: models do not remember the previous shot. Re-state wardrobe, props and time of day every time, and pass the previous approved frame as a reference when the tool allows.
Writing a screenplay and calling it a prompt: interior thoughts and backstory do nothing. Translate them into visible action, expression and light.
Indian settings rendered as generic 'India': name the city, architecture, fabrics and signage language (e.g. 'Lucknow old-city haveli, carved jaali screens, terracotta floor').

require.label: names shot size or camera movement

ban.label: vague quality tokens instead of camera/light specifics

cards.exemplar_brief: 30-second, 6-shot AI video ad prompt-script for a Lucknow chikankari brand's Diwali collection, 9:16, for a Seedance/Veo-class model with 5-second clips; one recurring model (woman, 28, wearing an ivory chikankari anarkali) and one location (old-city haveli courtyard at dusk with diyas); English prompts with one Hindi dialogue line; end card added in edit; goal: consistent, usable shots in at most two generations each.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Production-ready: header with model, 9:16, 6x5 s, look and generation budget; char/location bible with IDs and reference stills; every shot has timecode, shot size + movement, one timed action, lens/DoF, named light source and direction, audio, negatives and an anchor to the previous approved frame; Hindi line in quotes with speaker and language; titles and end card kept out of generation; AI-label plan and a product-truth check. Lucknow specifics (lakhori brick, jaali, tulsi platform, mogra) avoid generic 'India'.
