cards.name: Image alt text and accessible descriptions
cards.summary: The text a screen reader speaks in place of an image, also read by search engines. Good alt text gives the same information or function the image gives a sighted user, in context, in one short sentence; decorative images get an empty alt, functional images say what the link or button does.
use_for: alt text for website and ecommerce product images
alt text and image descriptions for Instagram, LinkedIn and X posts
accessible descriptions for charts and infographics (short alt + long description)
accessibility fixes in a website content audit
avoid: Starting with 'Image of' or 'Picture of': screen readers already announce it is an image. Start with the content.
Keyword stuffing ('kurta, cotton kurta, best kurta, buy kurta online'): it is spam to search engines and noise to screen-reader users. Describe the image; one natural keyword is enough.
Describing a logo-link as the logo ('Company logo'): for a linked image, say where it goes ('Home', 'Chat with us on WhatsApp').
Squeezing a chart into alt text: give a one-line takeaway in alt and put the data in a table or text near the chart.

sources.title: W3C WAI: An alt decision tree (fetched 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: decorative: empty alt; images of text: alt holds the text; functional images: alt gives destination or action; complex images: information elsewhere on the page; informative: brief description that conveys the meaning

sources.title: Google Search Central: Google Images best practices
sources.supports: descriptive alt text helps Google understand images

buyers: publishers and government/education sites with accessibility obligations
cards.value_why: Usually a small add-on to web, ecommerce or social work; no dedicated marketplace category found on 2026-10-04.
cards.goal: A screen-reader user gets the same information or function the image gives everyone else.

structure.does: Classify each image: informative, functional (inside a link/button), image of text, complex (chart, map), or decorative.
structure.length: a label per image, not published

structure.does: What matters about the image in this context: subject, key detail (colour, pattern, action, expression), setting if relevant.
The destination or action of the link or button, not the picture.
The text in the image, verbatim (or its key content if long).
Short alt with the takeaway plus a long description or data table on the page.
Empty alt (alt="") so screen readers skip it.

length.note: Per image. Context decides: the same photo needs different alt on a product page (colour, fabric) and in a news story (who, what event). Long descriptions go in body text or a caption, not alt.

checklist: Is each image classified (informative, functional, text, complex, decorative)?
Does no alt text start with 'image of' or 'picture of'?
Do decorative images have an empty alt?
Do linked or button images describe the destination or action?
Do images of text carry that text in the alt?
Does each informative alt include the detail that matters on this page (e.g. colour and pattern on a product page)?
Is each alt free of keyword lists?
Do charts have a takeaway alt plus data elsewhere on the page?
pitfalls: Same alt on every product image ('Blue kurta'): describe what each angle shows ('Back view showing the hand-embroidered yoke').
Repeating the caption in alt: screen-reader users hear it twice. If a caption already says it, keep alt short or describe what the caption does not.
Guessing people's identity, caste, religion or emotions: describe what is visible; name people only when the page names them.
Hindi or regional pages with English alt: write alt in the page's language so the screen reader voices it correctly.
cards.exemplar_brief: Alt text for 6 images on a Jaipur hand-block-print double bedsheet product page. Image 1 (front product shot): the double bedsheet spread on a bed with two matching pillow covers, off-white cotton ground, rust-red and indigo block print of small paisley (buta) motifs in staggered rows. Image 2 (close-up of the print): one rust-red paisley outlined in indigo dots, slightly uneven ink at the edges, cotton weave visible. Image 3 (size-chart image): text reads 'Double bedsheet 90 x 108 in (229 x 274 cm); 2 pillow covers 17 x 27 in (43 x 69 cm); 100% cotton, 144 thread count; wash cold, separately for the first wash'. Image 4 (lifestyle bedroom photo): the same sheet on a bed in morning light, a woman sitting cross-legged reading, cane bedside table with a brass lamp, white wall. Image 5 (decorative divider): thin green line with a small leaf in the middle, no text. Image 6 (linked icon): green WhatsApp icon with the words 'Chat on WhatsApp', opens a chat with the seller (Mon-Sat, 10 am-7 pm). English; one alt per image (empty for the decorative one), labelled by image; goal: a screen-reader shopper learns colour, pattern, size and how to contact the seller.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. All six images classified; informative alts carry colour and pattern, the close-up adds handmade cues (uneven ink, block overlap), size chart carries its text, decorative alt is empty, the WhatsApp link names the action; no 'image of'. Image 1 and 4 alts run 21-22 words, just over the card's 5-20 band. Colours/motif are stand-ins and sizes are placeholders because the brief gives none. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> describe what each image shows (ground colour, motif, lifestyle scene) and give the size-chart text (e.g. bedsheet and pillow-cover dimensions); alt text can only describe supplied visuals, so the writer had to invent indigo/lotus. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now describes what each of the 6 images shows and gives the size-chart text; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Amazon A+ content / Brand Story
cards.summary: The module-based, image-led section below an Amazon listing (A+ modules and the Brand Story carousel) available to brand-registered sellers. Good A+ copy is short benefit headlines and one-line explanations placed in images, plus a comparison chart of the brand's own range, so a shopper who scrolled past the bullets can decide without leaving the page.
use_for: A+ content (Enhanced Brand Content) for Amazon.in / Amazon.com listings
Brand Story carousel copy
comparison chart across a brand's own variants
rewriting A+ text after returns or Q&A show buyer confusion
avoid: Pasting the bullet points into modules: A+ should add what bullets cannot (how it works, who it's for, comparisons, care). Plan the modules from buyer questions.
Long paragraphs in image modules: shoppers skim on mobile. One headline plus 1-2 lines per tile.

Price, discount, shipping or ranking claims ('lowest price', 'best seller', '50% off'): they go stale and A+ content is reviewed against Amazon's content guidelines. Check the current guidelines in Seller Central before submitting.
Comparing against other brands by name: keep the comparison chart to your own range unless the guidelines allow otherwise.

sources.title: Amazon Seller Forums: guide to A+ modules
sources.supports: A+ content (Enhanced Product Description, Brand Story) is a separate module-based description for Brand Registry sellers (forum, low confidence)

sources.title: Fiverr: Product Descriptions subcategory
sources.supports: platform filter includes Marketplaces and App store (4945 gigs on 2026-10-04)

cards.value_why: Sold as a listing add-on by marketplace agencies; Fiverr's Product Descriptions category has a Marketplaces platform filter (4945 gigs, 2026-10-04). Module text limits and rules live in Seller Central, so the writer must work inside the builder's constraints.
cards.goal: Feel confident enough to add to cart without asking a question or leaving the page.

structure.does: Who the brand is, why it exists, what makes it trustworthy, and cards linking to other products.
The core promise in the shopper's words, matching the main image.
3-4 tiles, each a benefit headline with a one-line proof (material, test, measurement).
Ingredients, materials, process or tech explained simply, with what each does for the user.
2-4 situations or buyer types, each with why this product fits.
Own variants side by side: size, key spec, best for; helps shoppers pick and reduces wrong-variant returns.
Answers the top questions from the listing's Q&A and reviews.

length.note: Total text across modules. Module type and image count decide it; check each module's character limits in the A+ builder before writing.

checklist: Is every tile headline a benefit, not a feature name?
Does every claim rest on something measurable or verifiable (material, test, certification)?
Does the comparison chart cover only the brand's own range?
Is the copy free of price, discount, shipping and ranking claims?
Does at least one module answer a question found in the listing's Q&A or reviews?
Is every text block short enough to read on a phone in one glance?
Does the Brand Story say why the brand exists, not just what it sells?
Does the A+ add information the bullets do not already give?
pitfalls: Writing without the images: A+ copy and images are one unit. Get the image plan or write the image direction next to each text block.
Unproven 'dermatologically tested', 'chemical-free', 'clinically proven' claims: ask for the test report or cut the claim.
One A+ for every variant with different needs: a baby oil and a hair oil from the same brand need different modules.
Ignoring Hindi and regional shoppers: if the brand sells heavily in Hindi-speaking markets, ask whether a Hindi listing is planned and keep sentences simple for translation.

ban.label: price, promo or ranking claims that go stale

cards.exemplar_brief: A+ content (Brand Story with 4 cards + 5 modules including a comparison chart of 3 variants) for 'Nariyal Nest' (demo name), a Kochi coconut-oil-based baby massage oil brand on Amazon.in, founded 2021 by two Kochi mothers who could not find an oil without mineral oil or fragrance. Evidence supplied. Ingredients: virgin coconut oil 85%, sweet almond oil 10%, sesame oil 4%, vitamin E 1%; no mineral oil, fragrance or parabens. Safety: patch-tested on 52 babies aged 3 weeks to 18 months at an NABL-accredited lab (report dated June 2025), no irritation recorded; claim 'tested from 3 weeks', not 'newborn-safe' for younger babies. Absorption: in an in-house trial with 20 parents, 17 said the skin no longer felt oily after 10 minutes. Staining: oil left on white cotton for 2 hours, one 30 C wash with ordinary detergent removed it fully on 4 of 5 swatches, a faint mark stayed on 1. Variants (at about 7 ml per daily massage): 100 ml flip-cap travel bottle, about 2 weeks; 200 ml flip-cap bottle, about 4 weeks; 500 ml pump bottle, about 10 weeks. Buyer questions to answer: 'is it sticky?', 'safe for newborns?', 'does it stain clothes?'. Audience: first-time parents; English; 250-400 words of module text; goal: add to cart.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Re-test on the fixed brief. Brand Story 4 cards, hero, 3 benefit tiles that answer the three buyer questions with the supplied evidence (17 of 20 parents, 52 babies from 3 weeks at an NABL lab, 4 of 5 swatches clean), what's inside with the exact %, a who-it-is-for size module and a 3-variant own-range chart (14/28/70 massages at 7 ml check out); an honest 'tested from 3 weeks, ask your paediatrician' line; no price or ranking claims. Nits (writer): the newborn answer sits in a chart footnote rather than a tile or FAQ line; Module 3 repeats the founders' story from card 2; 'Check us, don't trust us' and '100% of the label' are awkward. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Anchoring / emcee script (events)
cards.summary: The compere's complete running script for a live event: announcements, opening, welcome of guests in protocol order, an intro and outro for every act, audience engagement, filler for delays, and the close. A good script keeps the event on time, gets every name and title right, and gives the anchor lines that are easy to say aloud.
use_for: school and college annual days, fests and farewells
corporate town halls, award nights and dealer meets
government and institutional functions
weddings, sangeet and family functions
product launches and cultural programmes
avoid: Writing paragraphs to be read: anchors speak in short breaths. Break lines at breath points and keep sentences short.
Guessing names, titles and order: a wrong designation in front of a chief guest is the classic failure. Mark every unconfirmed name [CONFIRM] and get the organiser to sign off the protocol list.
Borrowing famous shayari and misattributing it: popular couplets online are often credited to the wrong poet. Write original lines or cite verified sources.
Jokes about guests' looks, region, caste or religion: keep humour on the situation and the anchor.
buyers: corporate HR and internal comms teams
cards.value_why: Every Indian school, college, corporate and wedding event needs one, but it is mostly written by the anchor or event company; paid commissions are small.
cards.goal: Run the event on time in the right protocol order while keeping the audience engaged and every guest correctly honoured.

structure.does: Phones on silent, seating, exits, photography rules, start time.
Greeting in the event's languages, an original shayari or quote, the occasion and its purpose.
Each dignitary by full name and designation in the organiser's protocol order, with a one-line honour; cues for bouquets or mementos.
Lamp lighting, invocation, anthem or song, each with a clear spoken cue and a bracketed stage note.
For each item: who performs, what it is, one engaging line; after it, a thank-you and a bridge to the next.
Credentials relevant to the audience, and a handover line.
Quiz, claps, call-and-response, shayari or trivia ready for delays and stage changes.
Category, winner name, presenter, photo cue, in order.
Hand over to the vote of thanks, then final thanks, anthem if applicable, exit and dinner instructions.

length.note: Set by the running order and number of items; a 2-3 hour programme is typical. Time a read-aloud of the anchor's lines and keep the filler bank separate.

checklist: Is every guest name and designation either confirmed or marked [CONFIRM]?
Are guests welcomed in the organiser's protocol order?
Does every act have an intro and an outro line?
Are stage cues in brackets, separate from spoken lines?
Can each spoken sentence be said in one breath?
Is any shayari or quote original or correctly attributed?
Is there a filler bank of at least 4 items for delays?
Are language switches (Hindi/English) deliberate and balanced for the audience?
Is humour free of jokes about guests' looks, region, caste or religion?
Is the running time per segment noted?
pitfalls: No plan for delays: the chief guest arrives late at most Indian events. Write an alternate opening that does not need the chief guest present.
Over-praising every guest with the same adjectives: give each a specific line (their school, project, years of service).
Same bridge line between every act ('Let's give a big round of applause'): vary with callbacks to the previous act.
Forgetting stage logistics: who hands the memento, who comes up for the photo. Put it in brackets so the anchor can direct.

ban.label: stock anchor clichés
ban.regex: (?i)without (any )?further ado|ladies and gentlemen,? ladies and gentlemen

cards.exemplar_brief: Bilingual Hindi-English anchoring script for the annual day of a CBSE school in Patna: chief guest the district education officer and a guest of honour (names as [CONFIRM] placeholders), lamp lighting and Saraswati vandana, 8 cultural items, principal's address, prize distribution, vote of thanks; 2.5-hour programme; 1,800-2,500 words; includes an original opening shayari, intro and outro lines for every item and a 4-item filler bank; goal: run on time with every guest honoured correctly.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Runnable on the night: protocol order with [CONFIRM] names, timed running order that adds up to 2:30, alternate opening for a late chief guest, original two-line shayari, bracketed cues (bouquets, photo, lamp), intro and outro for all 8 items with varied callback bridges, prize sequence with presenters, 8-item filler bank (Pataliputra, Nalanda, Chhath), timekeeping cut rules. Hindi/English balance and register feel like a real Patna school stage; humour is safe. Nit: 'please stay standing for our national anthem' should be 'please stand'.

cards.name: Annual report narrative
cards.summary: The non-financial story of the year: the theme, the chairman's and CEO's letters, highlights and the business reviews. A good narrative tells shareholders plainly what happened, why, what went wrong, and what management will do next, and every number in it matches the audited statements.
use_for: chairman's message and MD/CEO letter
year-at-a-glance and highlights pages
business and segment reviews
theme line and section openers for listed companies, PSUs, NGOs and foundations
avoid: Only good news: shareholders and analysts already know the bad quarters. Name the miss, its cause and the response in the letter; it buys credibility for the rest.

Adjective-heavy prose ('robust performance amid headwinds'): replace with the number, the comparison and the reason ('Revenue rose 11% to Rs 2,140 crore; margins fell 3 points as solvent prices doubled').

Writing the statutory sections: the Board's Report, MD&A and sustainability disclosures follow formats owned by the company secretary, auditors and legal. The writer owns the narrative and keeps it consistent with them.
A theme that appears only on the cover: carry it into the letters and segment reviews or drop it.

sources.title: AWAI: 80 In-Demand Copywriting Projects (updated 2026-02-02)
sources.supports: lists Advertorial, Annual Report and Sales Enablement: Battlecard as priced copywriting project types

sources.title: Upwork: hire Report Writers
sources.supports: snippets list annual and sustainability reports (snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

buyers: listed companies' corporate communications and investor relations teams
cards.value_why: AWAI's 2026 copywriting pricing guide lists 'Annual Report' as its own project type, and Upwork's report-writer category lists annual and sustainability reports.
cards.goal: Understand what happened this year and why, and trust management's account of what comes next.

structure.does: A short phrase that captures the year's strategic story and recurs through the report.
Headline metrics with last year's figure and the change; one line on what drove each.
The year in context (economy, sector), the big decisions, what went wrong and what was learned, governance and people, outlook; signed.
Strategy, performance against last year's stated priorities, operations, next year's priorities with measurable targets where permitted.
For each segment: context, performance with numbers, drivers, outlook.
1-3 short features on a customer, plant, employee or community project, with named, consenting people.
The legal caution on forward-looking statements, as supplied by legal.

length.note: Narrative sections only. Driven by the number of segments, whether the report is integrated, and how many stories the company wants. A single chairman's letter commission is 800-1,500 words.

checklist: Does every number match the audited statements (with a page reference in the draft notes)?
Does each headline metric show last year's figure and the change?
Does the chairman's or CEO letter name at least one setback, its cause and the response?
Does each segment review cover context, performance, drivers and outlook?
Are last year's stated priorities reported against?
Is every vague adjective replaced by a number or a reason?
Is the forward-looking-statement caution included where outlook is discussed?
Does the theme recur beyond the cover?
Are named people in stories consenting and correctly titled?
pitfalls: Drafting before the numbers are final: annual reports change until the board approves the accounts. Mark every figure [VERIFY vs audited FS] and run a final number check.
Twelve hands, twelve voices: segment heads write differently. Apply one style sheet (number formats like 'Rs 2,140 crore', tense, titles) across all sections.
Promising targets legal has not cleared: write outlook as priorities unless guidance is formally given.
Copying last year's report with new numbers: analysts notice. Re-plan the narrative around this year's decisions.
cards.exemplar_brief: Chairman's message for the FY2025-26 annual report of 'Surya Fine Chem Ltd' (demo name), a mid-cap Gujarat specialty-chemicals company; chairman: Harshad Vora. Facts supplied (audited consolidated statements, pp. 118-124 of the report): revenue up 11% to Rs 2,140 crore (Rs 1,928 crore last year); EBITDA Rs 321 crore, margin down from 18% to 15% (last year Rs 347 crore) because raw-material costs rose faster than prices. Margin action: price-adjustment clauses added to contracts covering 60% of volume (25% before), and a second source qualified for the main intermediate. Dahej plant (Rs 410 crore project) commissioned in October 2025, six months late: delayed delivery of imported glass-lined reactors plus a three-month wait for the state pollution board's consent to operate; extra cost Rs 42 crore, mostly interest and site costs. First externally assured sustainability report (limited assurance). Dividend maintained at Rs 6 a share. Last year's stated priorities: commission Dahej by April 2025 (missed), raise export share from 31% to 35% (achieved: 36%), publish an assured sustainability report (done). Outlook target permitted: Dahej at 60% utilisation by March 2027; no margin guidance. Theme line: 'Chemistry of Resilience'. Audience: retail shareholders and analysts; English; 900-1,200 words; goal: shareholders trust management's account of a mixed year.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Candid, shareholder-first letter: strong opening ('sold more than ever before and earned less on each rupee'), margin fall owned as a contract-design weakness with a fix, Dahej delay addressed under its own head, assurance explained in plain terms, dividend reasoning, priorities-vs-results section, outlook as priorities, FLS caution; derived EBITDA (~321 vs ~347 crore) is correctly computed and flagged VERIFY. Writer faults: 'customers who had paused orders returned' and the record-sales implication are not in the brief; the theme line is a placeholder that never recurs in the letter. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply the Dahej delay cause, its cost and one margin action taken; the checklist demands setback + cause + response and the brief gives the cause for only one of the two setbacks, leaving ~20 [CONFIRM] slots. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now supplies the Dahej delay cause and cost, a margin action, prior-year priorities, outlook target, theme line and page references; re-judge pending.

cards.name: API reference documentation
cards.summary: Endpoint-by-endpoint (or function-by-function) reference a developer scans while coding. Good reference is complete, consistent and exact: every parameter typed and explained, a request that runs when pasted, a response that matches the schema, and every error paired with a fix.
use_for: REST/GraphQL endpoint reference pages
SDK and library function reference
webhook event reference
overview pages: authentication, errors, pagination, rate limits, versioning
avoid: Descriptions that repeat the name ('amount: The amount'): add units, limits, defaults and side effects ('Refund amount in paise; must not exceed the captured amount; defaults to the full amount').
Inventing parameters or behaviour: reference is generated from the spec (OpenAPI) plus engineer review. If the spec is silent, ask; never guess.
Tutorial prose inside reference: step-by-step journeys belong in a guide (genre:developer_tutorial); link to it.
Real keys or customer data in examples: use clearly fake placeholders.

sources.title: US BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: Technical Writers
sources.supports: 'The median annual wage for technical writers was $90,390 in May 2025.'

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide
sources.supports: industry style guide used for API and developer docs

sources.title: AmbitionBox: Technical Writer salary (updated 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: 'The average salary for a Technical Writer is ₹8.5 Lakhs per year' (10.1k salaries)

buyers: API-first SaaS and fintech companies (payments, UPI, KYC, logistics APIs)
cards.value_why: Technical writing is a BLS-tracked occupation with a May 2025 median wage of $90,390; in India AmbitionBox puts the average technical writer at ₹8.5 lakh a year (updated 2026-10-04), about double a content writer.
cards.goal: Make a correct first call and handle errors without opening a support ticket.

structure.does: Task-shaped name: verb + object ('Create a refund').
What the endpoint does, when to use it, key side effects (emails sent, money moved).
Method and path, required auth scheme or scope, required headers (idempotency key, version).
Path, query and body parameters: name, type, required/optional, default, constraints, description with units.
A curl call (and one SDK snippet if the product has SDKs) that runs when pasted with a test key.
Success status code and a schema table of returned fields; realistic example response matching the schema.
Each error code or status this endpoint returns, what it means, and how to fix it.
Idempotency, pagination, rate limits, versioning caveats that apply here; links to related endpoints and guides.

length.note: Per endpoint, excluding code blocks. Endpoints with many parameters or complex errors run long; the overview pages (auth, errors, pagination) are written once.

checklist: Does every parameter have type, required/optional status and a description that adds meaning beyond its name?
Are units, formats and limits stated (paise vs rupees, ISO 8601 dates, max lengths)?
Does the example request run as written with a test key?
Does the example response match the documented schema?
Does every documented error include a fix?
Are terms identical across endpoints (one name per concept)?
Is every parameter traceable to the spec or an engineer's confirmation?
Are all keys and personal data in examples placeholders?
Is it written in present tense and second person?
pitfalls: Documenting the happy path only: developers live in the errors. Get the real error list from engineering logs or the spec.
Examples drifting from the API: wire examples to tests or regenerate them from the spec on each release.
Mixing money units: Indian payment APIs often take paise; say so in every amount field and in the example.
Undated breaking changes: link each reference page to the changelog and version header.
cards.exemplar_brief: API reference page for 'Create a refund' (POST /v1/payments/{payment_id}/refunds) of 'PayDemo', a Bengaluru payment gateway (demo name). Base URL https://api.paydemo.example; auth: HTTP Basic with the test key id as username and key secret as password (placeholders in examples). Facts from the engineering spec: full and partial refunds, amount in paise (integer, minimum 100 paise = Rs 1, cannot exceed captured amount minus earlier refunds); refunds allowed within 180 days of capture; Idempotency-Key header required (up to 64 characters, remembered for 24 hours); optional notes object (up to 15 key-value pairs, key up to 40 characters, value up to 256 characters). Success: 201 Created with id (rfnd_...), payment_id, amount, currency (INR), status (pending | processed | failed), notes, created_at (Unix seconds). Four errors: 400 PAYMENT_NOT_CAPTURED; 400 AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURED; 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED (same key, different body); 400 REFUND_WINDOW_EXPIRED. Audience: backend developers at Indian D2C merchants; English; 300-600 words plus a curl example and JSON request/response; goal: a correct first refund call.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Clean, scannable reference: task title, side effects (settlement deduction, partial refunds), auth + required Idempotency-Key, typed parameter tables with paise and examples, curl with test-key placeholders, response schema matching the JSON, all 4 briefed errors with fixes, pending/webhook guidance, notes and related links; second person, present tense. Writer fault: minimum 100 paise is stated as fact while other unspecified limits are bracketed; base URL placeholder means the curl does not run as pasted. CARD FIX (minor): exemplar_brief -> give the base URL, refund window (days), minimum amount and notes limits, since the checklist requires every parameter to trace to a spec. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now gives base URL, refund window, minimum amount, notes and idempotency limits, auth and error codes; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Public apology statement
cards.summary: A statement from a brand or leader that says sorry for a specific harm, owns it without excuses, and says exactly what has been done and what will change. A good apology is short, plain, signed by a named senior person and gives affected people a way to get redress.
use_for: brand apology after a service failure, offensive ad or product defect
leader or creator apology for a remark or post
apology to customers after a data incident (with legal review)
the apology paragraph inside a longer crisis statement
avoid: Non-apologies ('we regret if anyone was offended', 'mistakes were made'): they read as evasion and get screenshotted. Say 'We are sorry that we...' and name the act.
Blaming a vendor, an intern or a 'technical glitch' as the whole story: own the outcome first; explain the cause only as part of the fix.
Lawyer-only drafts that admit nothing and say nothing: legal should review the facts, not remove the apology. Agree the factual wording, keep the sorry.
Using an apology when facts are still unknown: issue a holding statement (genre:crisis_statement) and apologise once you know what happened.

sources.title: Upwork: hire Corporate Communications Experts
sources.supports: dedicated hire category; snippets list crisis, internal and external communications (snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

buyers: consumer brands, apps and D2C companies
cards.value_why: Written inside crisis-communications engagements rather than bought alone (Upwork corporate communications category); high stakes, low volume.
cards.goal: Affected people and onlookers accept that the organisation understands what it did and believe the fix.

structure.does: First sentence says sorry for the specific act, in active voice.
Plain facts known so far: what, when, how many affected; no speculation.
Names the harm from the affected people's side (time lost, money, hurt, safety).
Concrete actions already taken, with dates.
Prevention steps and who is accountable, with timing.
How affected people get help: refund, replacement, contact route, timeline.
Named senior person and title.

length.note: Severity and the number of affected people drive length; the social-media version is a 40-80 word excerpt linking to the full statement.

checklist: Does the first sentence contain an explicit sorry or apology?
Does it name the specific act rather than 'recent events'?
Is it free of conditional phrasing ('if anyone was offended')?
Is it free of passive evasions ('mistakes were made')?
Does it name at least one action already taken, with a date?
Does it name at least one future change, with timing?
Does it tell affected people exactly how to get help?
Is it signed by a named senior person?
pitfalls: Apologising in English only when the harmed audience speaks Hindi or a regional language: publish the apology in their language too.
Deleting the offending post silently before apologising: acknowledge it was removed and why.
Promises the business cannot keep ('this will never happen again'): commit to specific checks instead.
Defensive 'context' paragraphs longer than the apology: keep explanation to one or two sentences.

ban.label: non-apology phrasing
ban.regex: (?i)if (anyone|we have|any of you) (was |were |have been )?(offended|hurt)|mistakes were made|regret any inconvenience|inconvenience caused

cards.exemplar_brief: Public apology from a Mumbai mithai-delivery D2C brand after about 1,400 Diwali gift-box orders arrived up to 3 days late and its support line went unanswered for 2 days; facts supplied: courier partner capacity failure, refunds of delivery fee already issued, a second courier added; audience: customers on Instagram, X and email, plus press; English with a one-line Hindi version; 180-260 words; signed by the founder-CEO; goal: customers believe the apology and know how to claim redress.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. First sentence apologises for both specific failures in active voice; facts (1,400 orders, up to 3 days, 2 silent days, courier capacity) without speculation; impact told from the customer's evening ('a puja, a visit to your parents'); 'That is on us, not on the courier' owns it; actions done (auto delivery-fee refund, second courier) and changes (capacity cap, named accountability); exact redress route with deadline; signed by founder-CEO; natural Hindi line. Nit: 'or damaged' widens the redress beyond the brief.

cards.name: App store listing copy
cards.summary: The words on an app's Google Play or App Store page: name, subtitle or short description, screenshot captions, promotional text, full description, keywords and what's new. Good listing copy says what the app does for whom in the first visible line, sells through the first two screenshots, and places search keywords naturally within each store's limits.
use_for: Google Play store listing (title, short and full description)
App Store product page (name, subtitle, promotional text, description, keywords)
screenshot caption sets
localised listings for Hindi and regional markets
ASO refresh after a feature launch
avoid: Describing features before saying what the app is for: the first line must say the job ('Split rent, food and trip costs with flatmates').

Keyword stuffing or competitor names in fields: stores restrict it and users distrust it. Use each keyword once where it reads naturally; Apple's keyword field must not repeat the app name or name other apps.
Writing to one store's limits and pasting into the other: Apple and Google fields and limits differ. Draft per store using the platform cards.
Unproven ranking or user-count claims ('India's No. 1 app', '10 million users') without a dated source.

sources.title: Fiverr: Product Descriptions subcategory
sources.supports: platform filter includes Marketplaces and App store (4945 gigs on 2026-10-04)

sources.title: Google Play Console Help: store listing
sources.supports: store listing fields and character limits

sources.title: Apple: Creating your product page
sources.supports: writing guidance per field; keywords must not repeat the app or company name or use other apps' names

buyers: app startups and product marketing teams
fintech, edtech, health and gaming studios
cards.value_why: Fiverr's Product Descriptions category lists 'App store' as a platform filter (2026-10-04); work is usually bundled with ASO keyword research.
cards.goal: Install the app.

structure.does: Brand plus the core job or keyword, within the store's limit.
The main benefit for the main user, in plain words.
One benefit per screenshot; the first two carry the pitch and are readable at thumbnail size.
What the app does, for whom, and why it beats the current way; must work alone before 'more'.
4-8 features each tied to what the user gets.
Security, data handling, licences or registrations that matter in the category, real ratings or awards with dates.
A plain invitation to try the core action.
Non-repeating keyword list within the byte limit; release notes that say what changed for the user.

length.note: Full description; most users never expand it, so the title, subtitle/short description and captions do most of the selling. Field limits are in plat:apple_app_store and plat:google_play_listing.

checklist: Do the name and subtitle/short description say what the app does in plain words?
Does the first screenshot caption state the main benefit?
Do the first lines of the description work without expanding 'more'?
Does each main keyword appear once, naturally, in a high-weight field?
Is every user, rating or award claim dated and sourced?
Are regulated claims (credit, returns, health, money games) accurate to the app's licences?
Does every field fit its store's limit?
Do the release notes say what changed for the user?
pitfalls: Machine-translated Hindi listings: they read wrong and rank poorly. Transcreate captions and the short description with natural Hinglish or Hindi.
Captions that describe the screen ('Dashboard screen'): say the benefit ('See who owes what at a glance').
Release notes reading 'Bug fixes and improvements' every time: name the fix users noticed.
Forgetting the promotional text (iOS) can be changed without a new release: use it for timely messages.

ban.label: unproven top-ranking claim
ban.regex: (?i)no\.? ?1 app|#1 app|best app (in india|in the world|ever)

cards.exemplar_brief: Google Play listing (title, short description, full description and 5 screenshot captions) for a Hyderabad UPI-linked expense-splitting app for flatmates and college trips; features supplied: split by item or share, UPI settle-up requests, monthly rent reminders, Hindi and English UI; audience: 18-28 urban Indians; English with Hinglish screenshot captions; full description 250-400 words; goal: install.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Title 28/30 and short description 79/80 fit Play limits and say the job; five Hinglish captions are natural and benefit-led ('Flat ka hisaab, bina jhagde ke', 'Rent ki date? Hum yaad dilayenge'); description opening works before 'more', features tied to outcomes, trust block states the app never holds money with a legal CONFIRM, one closing action, release-notes placeholder that bans 'bug fixes'. 'MADE FOR' block is the one generic stretch.

cards.name: Audio series / audio drama script
cards.summary: An episodic script for listen-only fiction where dialogue, narration and sound carry everything. A good episode establishes place by sound, keeps every speaker identifiable without visuals, turns the story several times, and ends on a cliffhanger that makes the next episode feel unmissable.
use_for: long-running serial fiction for Indian audio apps (Pocket FM, Kuku FM type)
audio drama and radio plays
branded audio series
adapting a novel or web series for audio
avoid: Visual-only action ('she nods', 'he looks at the letter'): the listener gets nothing. Turn it into sound, dialogue or a narrator line.
Recaps told as summary ('Last time, Meera found out...'): dramatise the cliffhanger again in a short scene.
Similar-sounding names (Rohan/Rohit, Priya/Piya): listeners cannot see spelling. Make names differ in first sound and syllable count.
Episodes that end at a calm moment: serial apps live on the next play. End on a question, a danger or a reveal.

sources.title: medianews4u (2025-09-17): Pocket FM brings AI-powered audio storytelling to India
sources.supports: over 30,000 AI audio series live; over 33,000 Indian users publish audio series each month; top writers projected to cross Rs 10 lakh a year

sources.title: AmbitionBox: Script Writer salary (updated 2026-10-03)
sources.supports: 'The average salary for a Script Writer is ₹5 Lakhs per year ... with 1 year of experience' (400 salaries)

buyers: Indian audio-series apps and their writer programmes
cards.value_why: Pocket FM reports over 30,000 AI audio series live, over 33,000 Indian users publishing each month and top writers projected above Rs 10 lakh a year (medianews4u, 2025-09-17); AmbitionBox puts an entry-level script writer at Rs 5 lakh a year.
cards.goal: Finish the episode and immediately play the next one.

structure.does: Re-enters the last cliffhanger in action, or opens on a gripping sound-led moment.
Each scene opens with a bracketed sound cue and a line that tells the listener where and who.
3-5 scenes, each with a goal, an obstacle and a turn; one main conflict advances.
A discovery or betrayal that changes what the protagonist wants or knows.
Ends mid-tension on one clear question the next episode answers.
Optional narrator line or tease of the next episode.

length.note: Per episode. Set by the app's target episode duration and narration pace; time a read-aloud of episode 1 to calibrate words per minute for this language and voice.

checklist: Is each scene's location established by a sound cue or line within its first lines?
Can every speaker be identified without visuals (names in dialogue, distinct voices)?
Is the script free of visual-only action?
Are sound and music cues bracketed and separate from spoken lines?
Is the recap dramatised rather than summarised?
Does the main conflict advance in this episode?
Do character names differ clearly in sound?
Does the episode end on one clear unanswered question?
Can each line be spoken in one breath?
pitfalls: Narrator doing all the work: listeners want scenes. Use narration for time jumps and inner stakes, not to describe dialogue.
Too many characters in one scene: keep to two or three speakers so voices stay distinct.
Literary Hindi in dialogue for a mass app: write everyday Hindustani that voice artists say naturally; save shuddh Hindi for characters who would use it.
Cliffhangers that the next episode cheats: pay off the danger honestly or listeners stop trusting the hook.

ban.label: visual-only action in an audio script

cards.exemplar_brief: Episode 1 of a 60-episode Hindi audio drama for an Indian audio-series app: in Kanpur, a leather-factory owner's daughter discovers on her engagement night that her fiancé's father is the man who bankrupted her own father; Devanagari Hindi in an everyday register, sound cues in English brackets; 1,500-2,000 words; goal: the listener plays episode 2.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Best in batch. Cold open plants a sound motif (ring tapping on glass, 'hisaab barabar') that pays off on stage; every scene opens on a sound cue that places it; speakers named in dialogue, distinct names; visuals carried by dialogue ('tum muskura rahi ho'); everyday Hindustani that voice artists can say; mid-episode reversal (father engineered the match) and a clean cliffhanger at the roof door with one question for episode 2. Timeline consistent (2012 -> 14 years, Mehar 12 -> 26). 1,548 words, inside the band.

cards.name: Author bio
cards.summary: A short third-person bio for a book jacket, retailer author page, festival programme or byline. A good one leads with the credential that makes this author worth reading on this book's subject, lists only real credits, adds one human detail and fits the slot it is written for, usually delivered in a one-line and a paragraph version.
use_for: back-flap and back-cover bios
Amazon/KDP and Goodreads author pages
query-letter bios
festival, panel and byline bios
avoid: Life story from childhood: readers want relevance. Lead with what qualifies the author for this book; keep one personal detail.
'Aspiring author', 'avid reader', 'passionate about writing': they signal amateur. State what the author has done.
Inflated or unverifiable credits ('award-winning' with no award named): name the award or drop the word.
One length for every slot: write a one-liner and a paragraph; query-letter bios stay short (Jane Friedman's guide puts them at 50-100 words).

sources.title: Jane Friedman: How to Write a Query Letter That Gets Manuscript Requests
sources.supports: query anatomy: story description 150-300 words, comps, bio 50-100 words; whole query about 200-450 words

cards.value_why: Usually bundled with a blurb, KDP description or launch package rather than sold alone.
cards.goal: Trust the author on this book's subject and remember one human detail about them.

structure.does: Name, the most relevant credential, and the book or series.
Opens the paragraph version with the expertise or experience behind this book.
Previous books, prizes, publications or roles, named and real.
Where the author lives or works, linked to the book's world if possible, plus one specific human detail.
Website or one social handle (for retailer and festival bios).

length.note: Slot-driven: byline and one-liner 15-30 words; jacket and author page 60-150; query letter 50-100 (Friedman).

checklist: Is it in third person (unless the brief asks for first person)?
Does the first sentence give the credential most relevant to this book?
Is every credit named and real?
Is it free of 'aspiring', 'avid reader' and 'passionate about'?
Is there one specific human detail?
Are both the one-line and paragraph versions delivered?
Does each version fit its slot's word budget?
pitfalls: Credentials that do not connect to the book: a doctor writing a thriller should say what in their work feeds the story, or keep the credential brief.
Jokey bios on serious nonfiction: match the book's register.
Stale bios on retailer pages: date-check credits and update when a new book launches.
Listing every social handle: one link the author actually maintains.
cards.exemplar_brief: Author bio in two lengths (one line of 15-30 words; a paragraph of 80-110 words) for Ibaphylla Marbaniang (demo name), a Shillong-based schoolteacher, for her debut English YA mystery 'The Hour of the Living Roots', set in Meghalaya's living-root-bridge villages. Credentials supplied: 14 years teaching English at a Shillong school; short story shortlisted in the Kathasetu National Short Story Contest 2022 (demo name); grew up in Sohra. One personal detail to use: she coaches the school's under-14 girls' football team on Saturday mornings. Third person; for the back flap and the Amazon author page; English; goal: readers trust her to tell this place's story.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. Both versions in budget (26 and 85 words), third person, Sohra and the root-bridge villages tie her to the book's world, the named contest shortlist is there, and the Saturday under-14 girls' football detail lands as the human close. Nits (writer): 'written by a teacher with 14 years of English classes ... behind her' and 'her short fiction has been noticed' are flat; 'She still teaches there' has a vague 'there'. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Award entry / award submission
cards.summary: A written case for an awards jury, answering the entry form's questions (typically objective, insight, idea, execution, results) inside strict word limits. A winning entry tells one clear story in its first lines and proves every result with a number, a time period, a source and a comparison against the objective.
use_for: marketing effectiveness awards (Effie-style entries)
creative, PR and digital award submissions
HR, CSR, sustainability and industry awards
startup and innovation award applications
avoid: Results without a baseline ('sales grew massively'): juries penalise vague claims. Give number, period, source and the comparison to the objective or category.
An insight that is a fact about the brand ('our oil is cold-pressed'): an insight is a human truth about the audience, with evidence.
Ignoring the form's order and headings: answer each question where the jury expects it.
Going over the word limit or padding to it: use the space for proof, not adjectives.

sources.title: Boost Awards: Award writing
sources.supports: dedicated award-entry writing agency

sources.title: Effie Awards: entry details
sources.supports: entries are written cases judged on objective, insight, idea and results

buyers: corporates entering HR, CSR or industry awards
cards.value_why: Dedicated award-entry writing agencies exist (Boost Awards) and Effie entries are judged on a written case, but commissions are seasonal and few.
cards.goal: Score high enough with the jury to be shortlisted.

structure.does: The whole story in one breath: challenge, idea, headline result.
The business problem and measurable objectives set before launch.
A human truth about the audience, with the research or data that revealed it.
The idea in one sentence, then why it answers the insight.
Channels, timeline, scale and craft choices that brought the idea to life.
Each result vs its objective: number, period, source, benchmark; other factors ruled out.

length.note: The entry form's limit governs every section; plan to it before drafting and never exceed it.

checklist: Does each section answer the form's question under its own heading, in the form's order?
Does the summary give challenge, idea and headline result?
Were the objectives measurable and set before launch?
Is the insight a human truth with evidence, not a product fact?
Does every result give number, period, source and comparison to objective or benchmark?
Are other factors (price cuts, distribution, seasonality) addressed?
Is every section within its word limit?
Is client permission confirmed for the data used?
pitfalls: Writing the entry after the deadline rush from memory: collect the results deck, research and media data first.
Vanity metrics as results (impressions, views): pair them with business outcomes the objective named.
The same entry pasted into every category: rewrite the emphasis to the category's criteria.
Agency-speak ('disruptive', 'clutter-breaking'): show what was new by describing it.
cards.exemplar_brief: Effie-style award entry for 'Keralam Oil' (demo name), a Kerala Ayurveda hair-oil brand's Onam regional campaign, regional-marketing category; a summary plus five headed sections (Challenge and objectives, Insight, Idea and strategy, Execution, Results). Facts supplied: objective set in June 2026 of +15% Kerala sales in Aug-Sep vs last year; achieved +22% while the category grew 6% (retail audit, same two months); no price change (Rs 185 for 200 ml), distribution unchanged at about 11,200 outlets. Insight from 40 consumer interviews: grandmothers' oiling ritual is how many Kerala women remember being cared for. Idea: the grandmother's Sunday oiling, retold as a film. Execution: a 90-second Malayalam film released 14 August 2026 on YouTube and Instagram; 24 Malayalam WhatsApp stickers (grandmother's lines); 6.8 million film views and 410,000 sticker shares by 30 September; regional-language radio for two weeks. Client has approved use of all figures. English; 700-900 words; goal: shortlist.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Jury-ready logic: one-breath summary, objective set before launch with source, insight framed as a human truth from the 40 interviews, single-sentence idea, results stated as number/period/source/objective and benchmark (22% vs 15% target, 16 points over a 6% category), price, distribution and seasonality addressed, permission line. Execution is thin because film/sticker specifics and reach are placeholders; the 'for every 100 units' gloss is padding for a jury. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> say 'a summary plus five headed sections' (the card's structure has six parts including Summary, so 'five headed sections' contradicts it) and supply execution specifics (film length, platforms, sticker count, reach figures). | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now says a summary plus five headed sections and supplies execution specifics (film length, platforms, sticker count, reach); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Playbook / practical guide (B2B)
cards.summary: A step-by-step operational guide (often gated) that shows a business buyer exactly how to do a job, with templates, checklists and worked examples. A good playbook is mostly doing, little arguing: every chapter ends with something the reader can do on Monday, and the vendor earns trust by being useful rather than by pitching.
use_for: gated lead-magnet playbooks for SaaS and B2B services
sales or marketing enablement playbooks
field guides and toolkits for a buyer's job (hiring, collections, compliance)
customer-success guides that drive adoption
avoid: Argument instead of action: if a chapter persuades rather than instructs, it belongs in a white paper (genre:white_paper).
Generic steps any blog lists ('define your goals'): add the template, the numbers and the worked example only a practitioner would know. Interview an SME.
Product pitch in every chapter: keep the product to examples where it genuinely fits and one closing CTA.
No usable artefact: a playbook without a template, checklist or script is an article.

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: freelance writing job types and typical Upwork rate bands (blog/web content $15-$35/hr; script writer $30-$56/hr); script projects include AI-generated or animated videos; ghostwriting/business-writing project lists

cards.value_why: Sold inside the same gated-content and ghostwriting work as ebooks and white papers (Upwork writing job types, 2026-01-21); no separate marketplace category.
cards.goal: Do the job using the playbook's steps and templates (and remember who taught them).

structure.does: Outcome and audience ('The collections playbook for Indian SME finance heads').

structure.part: Who it's for + what you'll be able to do
structure.does: Sets the reader, the starting situation and the end state.
One page with the whole method as a checklist for readers who skim.

structure.part: Chapters (one per step of the job)
structure.does: Each: why the step matters, numbered how-to, template or script, worked example with realistic numbers, common mistakes, 'do this Monday' action.
Copy-ready templates, scripts, calculators referenced in the chapters.
Soft CTA: demo, audit call, community or next playbook.

length.note: Driven by the number of steps in the job; a single chapter commission is 1,000-2,000 words. Templates and checklists count as part of the value, not padding.

checklist: Does every chapter end with a concrete action the reader can take this week?
Is there at least one copy-ready template, checklist or script?
Does each chapter include a worked example with realistic numbers?
Are steps numbered in the order they are performed?
Is a quick-start checklist near the top?
Is there visible first-hand input (named practitioner, own data, real example)?
Is the product mentioned only where it genuinely fits, with one closing CTA?
pitfalls: Templates that need the vendor's product to work: make them tool-agnostic so readers can use them anywhere.
US examples for an Indian audience: set the numbers in rupees, Indian timelines and Indian regulations.
Wall-of-text PDFs: use checklists, tables and call-out boxes; readers come back to a playbook, so make it scannable.
Steps without failure modes: each step should say what usually goes wrong and how to spot it.

require.label: has a usable template, checklist or numbered steps

cards.exemplar_brief: Chapter 2 of a 5-chapter gated playbook, 'Collecting overdue invoices without losing the client', for an Indian accounts-receivable SaaS; audience: finance heads at Rs 20-200 crore manufacturing SMEs; must include a 3-stage reminder email template set, a phone script for 60+ days overdue and an escalation checklist; English; 1,500-2,000 words; goal: the reader runs the process this month.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Mostly doing, little arguing: who-for and end state, 12-item quick start, numbered day-3/15/30/45/60 ladder, three copy-ready emails with escalating asks, a 60+ day call script branched by answer type, escalation checklist with correct NI Act s138 timelines and MSMED/Samadhaan pointer, worked example with correct maths (Rs 32.9 lakh/day, Rs 3.3 crore freed, ~Rs 36 lakh interest), failure modes, Monday plan, one soft CTA. Fully Indian (UTR, NEFT/RTGS, e-way bill, challan) and tool-agnostic.

cards.name: Competitive battle card
cards.summary: An internal one-to-two-page sheet that arms sales reps to win against one named competitor: where we win, where they win, trap-setting questions, objection responses with proof, and what never to say. A good card is accurate, dated, honest about the rival's strengths and scannable mid-call.
use_for: competitor-specific cards for B2B SaaS and IT services sales teams
quick reference during discovery and demo calls
onboarding new reps on the competitive landscape
win/loss learnings turned into talk tracks
avoid: Trash talk and unverified claims about the rival: cards leak to prospects and get forwarded. Use only public, verifiable facts with a source and date.
Pretending the rival has no strengths: reps lose credibility the first time a prospect disagrees. List their real strengths and how to reframe them.
Long prose: reps scan for 10 seconds mid-call. Use headings, short bullets and 'they say / you say' rows.
Undated cards: competitors change pricing and features; a stale card loses deals.

sources.title: AWAI: 80 In-Demand Copywriting Projects (updated 2026-02-02)
sources.supports: lists Advertorial, Annual Report and Sales Enablement: Battlecard as priced copywriting project types

buyers: IT services and consulting sales teams
cards.value_why: AWAI's 2026 copywriting pricing guide lists 'Sales Enablement: Battlecard'; mostly written in-house by product marketing, so freelance volume is small.
cards.goal: A rep finds the right answer in seconds and keeps the deal without discounting.

structure.does: Competitor name, last updated date, owner, sources used.
Where we win and the buyer type we beat them with.
Their target segment, pricing model, key strengths, recent changes.
3 differentiators, each with proof (metric, customer, feature demo).
Honest strengths and how to reframe or qualify around them.
Questions that make the prospect discover the rival's weak spot themselves.
'They say / You say / Proof' rows for the common objections.
Named switch stories or permitted anonymised wins; claims reps must never make.

length.note: One or two screens; more competitors means more cards, not a longer card.

checklist: Is there a last-updated date and are competitor facts sourced?
Are the competitor's real strengths listed?
Does each objection have a response and a proof point?
Are trap-setting items phrased as questions, not attacks?
Is every claim about the competitor public and verifiable?
Is it scannable in under 30 seconds (headings, short bullets)?
Does it fit on one or two screens?
Are customer proof points named or approved for anonymised use?
pitfalls: Feature-checklist wars: buyers care about outcomes. Translate each differentiator into what the buyer gets.
No owner: assign who updates it each quarter or after each pricing change.
Discounting as the default answer: give reps value-based responses before price.
Same card for every segment: an SMB buyer and an enterprise buyer weigh the rival differently; add a segment note if needed.

ban.label: defamatory or abusive language about the rival

cards.exemplar_brief: Battle card for 'PayKart HR' (demo name), a Pune HR-and-payroll SaaS for 50-500 employee Indian companies, against a larger national payroll provider referred to as 'Competitor X'. Header: owner Meera Kulkarni (product marketing), updated 5 Oct 2026, sources: X's public pricing page and our own call notes. Facts supplied: we win on statutory compliance automation (PF, ESI, PT across states) and WhatsApp payslips; they win on brand size and bundled accounting. Pricing per employee per month: ours Rs 95 all-in, no set-up fee; X lists Rs 70 payroll plus Rs 25 compliance add-on and a one-time Rs 40,000 set-up above 100 employees (so for 200 staff, year one costs about Rs 2.28 lakh with us vs Rs 2.68 lakh with X). Proof supplied: approved named switch story - Sahyadri Auto Components (demo), 180 staff, Chakan, switched January 2026: payroll run cut from 3 working days to 5 hours; WhatsApp payslip open rate 91% within 24 hours vs 38% for emailed PDFs. Approved anonymised: a 320-employee Gujarat textile firm cut payroll re-runs from 6% to 0.5% of runs. Other metrics: state PT changes live within 2 working days; average go-live 9 working days across the last 20 customers. Audience: inside-sales reps on discovery calls; English; 400-700 words with 5 'they say / you say' rows and 4 trap questions; goal: handle 'X is bigger and cheaper' without discounting.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Scannable and honest: dated header with owner and review cadence, one-line positioning, quick facts, three differentiators translated into outcomes (state PT slabs, shop-floor staff on WhatsApp), X's strengths conceded then qualified, four genuine discovery questions, five they-say/you-say rows that answer 'bigger and cheaper' with a whole-cost comparison instead of a discount, never-say list. Every proof point and X fact is a placeholder. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply at least one approved switch story and one metric (e.g. hours saved per payroll run, WhatsApp payslip open rate); the checklist requires a proof point per objection and the brief gives none, so all five proofs became placeholders. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now supplies pricing for both sides, one named and one anonymised switch story and several metrics for the proof points; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Best-of roundup (ranked product list)
cards.summary: A ranked list of the best products for a use case: quick picks up top, then each pick with why it made the list, who it suits, what testing showed and its trade-off, plus a comparison table and buying guide. Google's review guidance asks for first-hand evidence and justified 'best' picks, so a good roundup reads like a tester's notes, not a catalogue.
use_for: 'Best X for Y' affiliate articles
gift guides and seasonal buying guides
'Top tools for [job]' SaaS roundups
commerce-desk listicles for publishers
avoid: Ten near-identical products from one marketplace page: each pick needs a distinct use case and a reason. Fewer, well-justified picks beat a long list.
Picks you never evaluated: Google's review guidance asks reviewers to show evidence of hands-on use and to justify 'best'. If you only researched specs, say so and frame the piece accordingly.
A list with no cons: every pick needs its trade-off and who should skip it.
Hiding affiliate relationships: disclose before the first link.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Write high quality reviews (last updated 2025-12-10)
sources.supports: firsthand evidence, quantitative measurements, pros and cons, comparison to alternatives, justify 'best' picks; ranked lists need enough useful content to stand alone

sources.title: Fiverr: Articles & Blog Posts category (Article type facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: supply signal by article type: Review 679 gigs, Affiliate marketing 323, Listicle 1243, Long-form 3494 (2026-10-04)

cards.goal: Pick the product that fits their use case and click through to buy it.

structure.does: 'Best [product] for [use case] ([year])' or a variant with the buyer's constraint (budget, space).
Plain affiliate disclosure before the first link.
Top 3-6 picks as 'Best overall / Best budget / Best for X', one line each with price and link.
Criteria, hands-on time, measurements and who tested.
For each: verdict line, who it's for, what testing showed (numbers), pros, cons, price with date, alternative.
Picks side by side on the 4-6 criteria that matter.
What to look for, mistakes to avoid, 3-6 real buyer questions.
Last tested/updated date and what changed.

length.note: Number of picks (5-10) and testing depth drive length; each pick must earn its section.

checklist: Does each pick name a distinct use case ('best for X')?
Is each 'best' justified with evidence from testing or stated criteria?
Is the testing or selection method stated?
Does every pick list at least one con?
Are prices given with the date checked?
Is there a comparison table?
Does an affiliate disclosure appear before the first link?
Is a last-updated date visible?
pitfalls: Ranking by commission rate: readers and Google notice when the 'best' pick is always the highest-paying one. Rank by fit and evidence.
Never updating: models go out of stock and prices move. Schedule a refresh and keep an update log.
Ignoring Indian buying factors: service network, warranty claims, voltage and water quality (for appliances), EMI and exchange offers matter to Indian buyers.
Copy-pasted spec bullets per pick: translate specs into what they mean for the use case.

cards.summary: A standalone article on a brand or creator site that answers one reader question well enough to earn search, AI-answer or social traffic. thought-leadership and opinion posts on a company blog

posts written to be cited by AI search answers
avoid: Throat-clearing intros ('In today's fast-paced world...', 'In this article we will...'): answer the question in the first two or three sentences.

Rewriting the top 10 search results: commodity content is what AI Overviews and scaled-content enforcement hurt. Add something only this business knows: a client example, own numbers, a photo, a practitioner quote.
Keyword-stuffed headings: write each H2 as the question or claim the section answers, with the keyword where natural.

structure.does: Key takeaways or a short checklist for skimmers.
One next step and 2-4 descriptive internal links.

length.note: Search intent drives it: a quick-answer query needs 700-1,000 focused words; a comparison or guide runs longer. Length that does not add answers hurts.

checklist: Does the title contain the main keyword and a clear promise?
Do the first 100 words answer the core question?
Is each H2 a question or claim that its section answers?
Is there at least one first-hand element (own data, client example, photo, expert quote)?
Are facts and numbers sourced?
Are there 2-4 internal links with descriptive anchor text?
Is there exactly one primary CTA?
Are a meta title and description supplied?
Is it free of throat-clearing intros and 'In conclusion' endings?
pitfalls: Writing for the keyword tool instead of the reader: check what the searcher actually wants (definition, steps, comparison) before outlining.
No author or reviewer: add a byline with relevant credentials, especially for money, health and legal topics.
Publishing and forgetting: plan a refresh when facts, prices or rules change (genre:content_refresh).

cards.name: Book blurb / back-cover copy
cards.summary: The few paragraphs on the back cover, jacket flap or retailer page that make a browser open the book. Fiction blurbs set up protagonist, want, obstacle and stakes and stop before the ending; nonfiction blurbs name the reader's problem, promise specific takeaways and prove the author can deliver.
use_for: back-cover and jacket-flap copy
retailer descriptions (Amazon, Flipkart) adapted from the blurb
series blurbs and box-set copy
publisher catalogue and festival listings
avoid: Plot summary of the whole book: stop at the end of act one, on the question the book answers.
Self-praise ('a gripping page-turner', 'unputdownable'): let real, permissioned endorsements say that, or show it through stakes.
Character lists and world-building lore: one protagonist, one antagonist or obstacle, one setting detail.
Fake or unpermissioned endorsement quotes: they mislead buyers; use only real quotes the endorser approved.

cards.goal: Open the sample or the first page, then buy.

structure.does: One line that states the hook or central question.
Who she is and where, with one specific detail.
What happens and what the protagonist now wants.
What stands in the way and what she loses if she fails.
A tension line or question; never the ending.
The reader's problem in their words, then what the book will help them do.
3-5 specific takeaways.
Author credential (nonfiction) or real, permissioned endorsement (either).

length.note: Cover space and genre drive it: thrillers and romance run short and punchy, literary fiction and nonfiction a little longer. Retailer pages can carry a longer version.

checklist: Fiction: is the protagonist named in the first two sentences?
Fiction: are the want, the obstacle and concrete stakes all stated?
Fiction: is the ending withheld?
Does the vocabulary signal the genre (crime, romance, fantasy, self-help)?
Nonfiction: is the reader's problem in the first line and are 3-5 specific takeaways named?
Is every endorsement real and permissioned?
Does it end on tension or a clear promise?
Does it fit the cover's word budget?
pitfalls: Opening with the setting's history: start with the person and the problem.
Vague stakes ('everything she holds dear'): name the thing she loses (the boat, her brother, her licence).
Translated fiction that reads translated: write the English blurb fresh for the English reader, keeping cultural specifics.
Comp titles on the cover without the publisher's agreement: keep comps for queries and retailer copy if the client prefers.

ban.label: self-praise clichés (leave praise to real endorsers)
